rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disclaimer is maximally fair: believers call their inevitable slips crimes, while opponents' grave disbelief is called mere deeds.
rows.anchor: الأجرام المنسوب إلى النفس بصيغة الماضي الدالة على التحقق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Past tense presents the believers' crimes as established; present tense for opponents' actions does not presuppose them.
rows.anchor: الأجرام المنسوب إلى النفس بصيغة الماضي الدالة على التحقق

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say the verse contains an indirect allusion, which does not compromise the fairness just described.
rows.anchor: وذكر أن في الآية تعريضا وأنه لا يضر بما ذكر

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some classify the verse as leaving the dispute and claim the sword verse abrogated it.
rows.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أنها من باب المتاركة وأنها منسوخة بآية السيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This resumes and confirms the preceding argument by exposing the true state of those invoked.
rows.anchor: إستئناف مقرر لما قبله كاشف عن جلية حال ما يدعونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For idol worshippers, idols cannot hear because lifeless objects have no capacity for hearing.
rows.anchor: بأنه جماد ليس من شأنه السماع هذا إذا كان الكلام مع عبدة الأصنام

rows.speaker: البلخي
rows.claim: If the invoked include Jesus or other close servants, their not hearing may result from being occupied and far from the caller.
rows.anchor: وبعد بعيد عن عابده كعيسى عليه السلام وروى هذا عن البلخي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He has no transmitted proof that angels or sanctified souls hear appeals from non-idolatrous callers; reason permits it but cannot establish it.
rows.anchor: إذ لم أظفر بدليل سمعي على ذلك والعقل يجوزه لكن لا يكتفي بمجرد تجويزه في القول به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hypothetical hearing does not entail a spoken answer, since idols lack speech; alternatively, they cannot act at all and cannot benefit callers.
rows.anchor: لأنهم لم يرزقوا قوة التكلم والسماع لا يستلزم ذلك فالمراد بالإستجابة الإستجابة بالقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For close servants, verbal response is impossible because callers falsely treat them as deities; practical aid is not their duty.
rows.anchor: فكيف يجيبون زاعم ذلك فيهم وفيه من التهمة ما فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The previous rationale, that answering would diminish servitude, may also explain their refusal to act.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون هذا تعليلا للأول أيضا فتأمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Resurrection idols disown the worshippers' association, either by speaking after God enables them or through an unmistakable display of their state.
rows.anchor: يجحدون إشراككم إياهم وعبادتكم إياهم وذلك بأن يقدر الله تعالى الأصنام على الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhu al-Rummah's speaking ruins illustrate how lifeless stones may seem to address someone through their condition, supporting disavowal by state.
rows.anchor: وقفت على ربع لمية ناطق يخاطبني آثاره وأخاطبه وأسقيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the invoked are angels or other close servants, their repudiation is clear; the preceding sura depicts angels denying that polytheists worshipped them.
rows.anchor: وقد حكى الله تعالى قول الملائكة للمشركين في السورة السابقة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada and others identify the uniquely informed reporter as God, who knows the reality of things; this confirms the idols' non-divinity.
rows.anchor: يعني به تعالى نفسه كما روى عن قتادة وغيره فإنه سبحانه الخبير بكنه الأمور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address may apply to any listener: no informant equals the all-knowing expert whose knowledge omits nothing in earth or heaven.
rows.anchor: لا يخبرك أيها السامع كائنا من كنت مخبر هو مثل الخبير

rows.speaker: إبن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya suggests the idols themselves are expert informants since they disclosed that they are not gods; al-Alusi calls this far-fetched.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يبكون ذلك من تمام ذكر الأصنام كأنه قيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People need God for their existence and every important matter; the definite plural intensifies their pervasive need, making other creatures' need seem negligible.
rows.anchor: في أنفسكم وفيما يعن لكم من أمر مهم أو خطب ملم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human weakness supports this reading; jinn need less for food and clothing and are not weak in the same way, so need not be included.
rows.anchor: ولا يرد الجن إذ هم لا يحتاجون في المطعم والملبس وغيرهما كما يحتاج الإنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if jinn are excluded, the address may target people who display strength and stubbornness; restricting poverty to comparison with God is unpersuasive.
rows.anchor: إذ الكلام مع من يظهر القوة والعناد من الناس والقول أن القصر إضافي بالنسبة إليه تعالى لا يخفى ما فيه

rows.speaker: صاحب الفرائد
rows.claim: The author of al-Fara'id includes humans and other beings, using the present over the absent and the superior over others; al-Alusi calls this very remote.
rows.anchor: صاحب الفرائد : الوجه أن يقال والله تعالى أعلم المراد الناس وغيرهم

rows.speaker: العلامة الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi reads people as a contextual reference to those addressed in 35:13, and poverty generically: they are the creatures most in need of God; al-Alusi finds this appealing.
rows.anchor: الذي يقتضيه النظم الجليل أن يحمل التعريف في الناس على العهد وفي الفقراء على الجنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone is free of need and is benefactor of all beings, deserving praise for His beneficence; hamid originally means praised.
rows.anchor: المنعم على جميع الموجودات المستحق بأنعامه سبحانه للحمد وأصله المحمود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God Praiseworthy completes the account of human need: wealth benefits the needy only when its owner is generous and beneficent.
rows.anchor: وأريد به ذلك على طريق الكناية ليناسب ذكره بعد فقرهم إذ الغني لا ينفع الفقير إلا إذا كان جوادا منعما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ka'b al-Ghanawi's line about a forbearing man respected by an enemy illustrates the praiseworthy sense of hamid.
rows.anchor: قول كعب الغنوي : حليم إذا ما الحلم زين أهله

rows.speaker: العلامة الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Tibi says God is independent of the addressees and their worship, since other servants praise Him; al-Alusi prefers the broader reading.
rows.anchor: وهو سبحانه غني عنكم وعن عبادتكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reported occasion says that after the Prophet prayed persistently and unbelievers persisted in rejection, they wondered whether God needed their worship; the verse was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: وما روى في سبب النزول من أنه لما كثر من النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم الدعاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: That reported occasion does not require narrowing the verse to that circumstance.
rows.anchor: لا يقتضي شيئا من التخصيص في الآية كما لا يخفى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sending of two is placed in the story to complete its parable and console the Prophet.
rows.anchor: بناء على أنه كان أمره تعالى لتكميل التمثيل وتتميم التسلية

rows.speaker: إبن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Ka'b say the two were messengers sent by God; a distinguished scholar chose this view and said they supported Jesus and confirmed his law, like Aaron supported Moses.
rows.anchor: إبن عباس وكعب هم رسل الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The divine-messenger view is supported by the wording that God sent them and by the people's objection that they were human, assuming divine messengers must not be human.
rows.anchor: وأيد بظاهر ( إذ أرسلنا إليهم إثنين )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some cite reports of miracles such as healing the blind and reviving the dead, since miracles properly belong to prophets.
rows.anchor: وأستدل البعض على ذلك بظهور المعجزة كإبراء الأكمه وأحياء الميت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opponents answer that the apostles may have spoken as direct envoys or been treated as representatives; reported miracles could be Jesus's confirming wonder through them, not proof they claimed direct divine mission.
rows.anchor: ومن ذهب إلى الأول أجاب عن الأول بما سمعت وعن الثاني بأنهم إما أن يكونوا دعوهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Reports name the two as Yuhanna and Bulus; Tuman and Bulus according to Muqatil; Shimon and Yuhanna by Shu'ayb al-Jubba'i; Sadiq and Saduq by Wahb and Ka'b; or Nazoos and Maroos.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل تومان وبولس وقال شعيب الجبائي شمعون ويوحنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The text says they were sent to the people rather than to the town, because sending properly takes people as destination and this prepares for their rejection.
rows.anchor: ليطابق إذ جاءها لأن الإرسال حقيقة إنما يكون إليهم لا إليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rejection attaches more clearly to people as object; the explanatory fa resembles Moses striking the stone, after which water gushed forth.
rows.anchor: نظير التعقيب في قوله تعالى : ( فقلنا أضرب بعصاك الحجر فأنفجرت )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The village inhabitants were idol worshippers; azzazna means God strengthened and reinforced the two.
rows.anchor: فعززنا ( أي قويناهما وشددنا قاله مجاهد وإبن قتيبة

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and Ibn Qutayba gloss the verb as strengthening; other lexicographers give related senses of flesh hardening and rain compacting earth.
rows.anchor: قاله مجاهد وإبن قتيبة وقال يقال تعزز لحم الناقة إذا صلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb omits its object, understood as the two messengers from the preceding clause; the third as means of reinforcement is the point.
rows.anchor: لدلالة ما قبله عليه ولأن المقصود ذكر المعزز به

rows.speaker: إبن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the third was Shimon al-Safa, also called Samaan; Wahb and Ka'b call him Shalum; Shu'ayb al-Jubba'i gives Bulus, spelled with sad by him and sin by some.
rows.anchor: على ما روى عن إبن عباس شمعون الصفا ويقال سمعان أيضا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan, Abu Haywa, Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal, and Aban read without doubling the zay; the light and doubled forms are synonymous.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وأبو حيوة وأبو بكر والمفضل وأبان ( فعززنا ) بالتخفيف

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu Ali derives the light form from azzahu, to overcome, invoking the proverb that whoever overcomes takes spoils; the third's proof defeated the opponents.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي المخفف من عزه إذا غلبه ومنه قولهم من عزيز أي من غلب سلب

rows.speaker: عبدالله
rows.claim: Abdullah reads with the phrase bil-thalith, with the third.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبدالله بالثالث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fa coordinates their statement after denial and reinforcement; plural attribution works if all agreed, even if one spoke while the rest concurred.
rows.anchor: عطف على فكذبوهما فعززنا والفاء للتعقيب أي فقال الثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After their arguments failed, the people called the messengers ill omens, following ignorant habits of favoring what suits desire and fearing what does not, regardless of actual good or harm.
rows.anchor: لما ضاقت عليهم الحيل وعييت بهم العلل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, they feared the warning of harm if they did not believe, so they recoiled from the call.
rows.anchor: أو بناء على أن الدعوة لا تخلو عن الوعيد بما يكرهونه من إصابة ضر إن لم يؤمنوا

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says rain was withheld from the people.
rows.anchor: مقاتل : إنه حبس عنهم المطر

rows.speaker: آخر
rows.claim: Another report says leprosy spread quickly among them after they rejected the messengers.
rows.anchor: آخر : اسرع فيهم الجذام عند تكذيبهم الرسل

rows.speaker: إبن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya attributes their superstition to division and discord among the people; the wording indicates the preaching triggered it.
rows.anchor: إبن عطية : أن تطير هؤلاء كان بسبب ما دخل فيهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their threat means the messengers must stop making this statement.
rows.anchor: أي عن مقالتكم هذه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the threatened stoning means killing with stones, though it could instead mean harming them by stoning.
rows.anchor: بالحجارة قاله قتادة وذكر فيه احتمالان إحتمال أن يكون الرجم للقتل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid, in a report from Abd ibn Humayd, interprets rajm as cursing or insulting, and says rajm throughout the Qur'an means insult.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد أنه قال : أي لنشتمنكم

rows.speaker: البحر
rows.claim: Al-Bahr glosses the painful punishment as burning; another opinion says it leaves its victims alive.
rows.anchor: في البحر : وهو الحريق وقيل عذاب غيره تبقى معه الحياة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threats can mean stoning them to death or excruciating punishment if they survive; alternatively, the threats may be bodily and spiritual, with assignments reversed in another view.
rows.anchor: والمراد لنقتلنكم بالحجارة أو لنعذبنكم إذا لم نقتلكم عذابا أليما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This passage disproves resurrection denial from what people observe in themselves, just as the preceding argument disproved associating partners from signs in their possessions.
rows.anchor: مسوق لبيان بطلان إنكارهم البعث بعد ما شاهدوا في أنفسهم ما يوجب التصديق به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A proposed reading treats the verse as consolation to the Prophet about their words, like 36:76; al-Alusi says that does not fit.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إنه تسلية له عليه الصلاة والسلام كقوله تعالى ( فلا يحزنك قولهم )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hamza conveys denial and wonder; the waw coordinates with an implied sentence that entails the question, as in the earlier question at 36:71.
rows.anchor: والهمزة للإنكار والتعجب والواو للعطف على جملة مقدرة هي مستتبعة للمعطوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question may repeat the previous denial rhetorically and prepare a stronger one: people should know their own creation, the clearest and most important fact about themselves.
rows.anchor: أو هي عين تلك الجملة أعيدت تأكيدا للنكير السابق وتمهيدا لإنكار ما هو أحق منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The scholars link both questions through inversion: God made provision for people to be thanked but they disbelieved, and made them from lowly fluid for humility but they became arrogant and disputatious.
rows.anchor: فإنه تعالى خلق للإنسان ما خلق ليشكر فكفر وجحد المنعم والنعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The generic word human is used rather than a pronoun because the question concerns human nature and behavior.
rows.anchor: وإيراد الإنسان مورد الضمير لأن مدار الإنكار متعلق بأحواله من حيث هو إنسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase presents the human as suddenly becoming an emphatic, open disputant in false argument.
rows.anchor: أي مبالغ في الخصومة والجدال الباطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God created humans from something low and vile, yet they suddenly dispute a matter whose truth their own origin plainly witnesses.
rows.anchor: ظاهر متجاهر في ذلك عطف على الجملة المنفية داخل في حيز الإنكار والتعجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mubin is transitive, describing a disputant who makes his inner thoughts clear.
rows.anchor: مبين ) متعد والكلام من متممات شواهد صحة البعث

rows.speaker: ابن مردويه
rows.claim: A narration attributed to Ibn Abbas through Ibn Mardawayh identifies the challenger as Ubayy ibn Khalaf, whom the Prophet killed at Uhud with a spear; Abu Malik, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Suddi, Ikrima, and others report that identification.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية ابن مردوية عنه أن الجاني القائل ذلك أبي بن خلف

rows.speaker: إبن عباس
rows.claim: Other reports from Ibn Abbas name Abu Jahl or Abd Allah ibn Ubay; Abu Hayyan rejects the latter attribution because the sura is Meccan and Abd Allah ibn Ubay never made such an open challenge.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية أخرة عن الحبر أنه أبو جهل بن هشام وفي أخرى عنه أيضا أنه عبد الله بن أبي

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan chooses Ubayy ibn Khalaf as the soundest identification, while allowing each named unbeliever may have made the challenge.
rows.anchor: والذي اختاره وادعى أنه أصح الأقوال أنه أبي بن خلف ثم قال : ويحتمل

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and Qatada are also reported to identify Umayya ibn Khalaf as the challenger.
rows.anchor: وحكى عن مجاهد وقتادة أنه أمية بن خلف

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative reads this as the sudden result of creation: after insignificant fluid, the human becomes discerning and eloquent, able to argue.
rows.anchor: فإذا هو بعدما كان ماء مهينا رجل مميز منطيق قادر على الخصام

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: On that reading, the clause coordinates with created him, the sudden transition refers to creation, and mubin is transitive.
rows.anchor: فهو حينئذ معطوف على خلقناه والتعقيب والمفاجأة ناظران إلى خلقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominal sentence marks persistent disputation; the suddenness intensifies astonishment at that transformation.
rows.anchor: إسمية للدلالة على استقراره في الخصومة واستمراره عليها

rows.speaker: إبن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas says al-As ibn Wa'il brought the Prophet a decayed bone, crumbled it, and asked whether God could revive it; the Prophet said God would raise it, then cause him to die, revive him, and enter him into Hell, whereupon these verses to the sura's end were revealed.
rows.anchor: أخرج جماعة منهم الضياء في المختارة عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause coordinates with the negative clause under one reading, or with the sudden-result clause under the alternative.
rows.anchor: معطوف على حينئذ على الجملة المنفية داخل في حيز الإنكار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression may mean an astonishing story denying resurrection, an absurd fable in his view, or making humans a likeness for God and measuring divine power by human power.
rows.anchor: أي أورد في شأننا قصة عجيبة في نفس الأمر هي في الغرابة كالمثل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He forgot God's creation of him; the phrase may coordinate with the preceding clause or be circumstantial, and forgetting may mean failing to recall, willfully neglecting, or acting as if forgotten.
rows.anchor: أي خلقنا إياه على الوجه المذكور الدال على بطلان ما ضربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standalone he said answers an implied question about what parable he offered or what he said.
rows.anchor: استئناف وقع جوابا عن سؤال نشأ من حكاية ضربه المثل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He denies anyone could revive bones and highlights their extreme decay by calling them ramim.
rows.anchor: منكرا ذلك ناكرا من أحوال العظام ما تبعد معه من الحياة غاية البعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Apparently ramim is an adjective, either active from intransitive decay or passive and common to masculine and feminine.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن رميم صفة لا إسم جامد فإن كان من رم اللازم بمعنى بلى

rows.speaker: محي السنة
rows.claim: Muhyi al-Sunna says ramim lacks feminine marking because it is altered from a feminine form, like baghiy in 19:28 from baghiya.
rows.anchor: محي السنة : لم يقل رميمة لأنه معدول من فاعلة

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azhari says bones follow a singular pattern like kitab and qirab, so the adjective is singular masculine; al-Alusi calls this unusual.
rows.anchor: الأزهري : إن عظاما لكونه بوزن المفرد ككتاب وقراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If ramma is transitive, meaning to make decay, ramim is passive; the root evokes eating, so the earth consumed what decayed.
rows.anchor: وإن كان من رم المتعدي بمعنى أبلى يقال رمه أي أبلاه وأصل معناه الأكل

rows.speaker: المطلع
rows.claim: Al-Mutli' treats ramim as a noun like rimma and rufat, not an adjective; al-Alusi doubts this because it has a verb and adjectival pattern.
rows.anchor: وفي المطلع الرميم اسم غير صفة كالرمة والرفات لا فعيل بمعنى فاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command rebukes the objector by recalling evidence in his nature and directing him to reason from it.
rows.anchor: تبكيتا له بتذكير ما نسيه من فطرته الدالة على حقيقة الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The One who first brought the bones into being and developed them will revive them; re-creation is easier than originating them without precedent.
rows.anchor: إذ لم يسبق لها إيجاد ولا شك أن الإحياء بعد أهون من الإنشاء قبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No incapacity can arise in God, since His power is essential and eternal and cannot cease or change.
rows.anchor: ولا احتمال لعروض العجز فإن قدرته عز وجل ذاتية أزلية لا تقبل الزوال ولا التغير

rows.speaker: الفارابي
rows.claim: Al-Farabi wished Aristotle had seen the syllogism: whoever first creates can recreate and revive; God first created and animated the bones, so He can restore them with their powers.
rows.anchor: كان الفارابي يقول وددت لو أن أرسطو وقف على القياس الجلي في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse appears to support the Shafi'i position, also attributed to Malik and Ahmad, that bones receive life and undergo death; carrion bones are then impure.
rows.anchor: والآية ظاهرة فيما ذهب إليه الإمام الشافعي قيل ومالك وأحمد من أن العظم تحله الحياة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether bones receive life is disputed among jurists and philosophers; proponents of no life argue that life entails sensation while bones feel no pain when cut.
rows.anchor: مما اختلف فيه الفقهاء والحكماء واستدل من قال منها بعدم حلولها فيه بأن الحياة تستلزم الحس

rows.speaker: إبن زهر
rows.claim: Ibn Zuhr says Galen's remarks on bone sensation are inconsistent, and concludes bones have slow sensation because animal spirit prevents their decay during life.
rows.anchor: ابن زهر في كتاب التيسير : اضطرب كلام جالينوس في العظام هل لها إحساس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some jurists say bones have no life and stay pure after death; they read bones as their owner or revival as restoring them to living moist form, but al-Alusi says those readings depart from the apparent sense.
rows.anchor: فحيث لم تحلها الحياة لم يحلها الموت فلم تكن نجسة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other jurists accept the verse as evidence bones have life but still regard them as pure, because carrion impurity comes from moisture and flowing blood, which bones lack.
rows.anchor: ومن الفقهاء القائلين بعدم نجاسة عظام الميتة من رأى قوة الإستدلال بالآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows every created thing, including each person's scattered fragments and how parts were connected, separated, gathered, or dispersed.
rows.anchor: مبالغ في العلم فيعلم جل وعلا بجميع الأجزاء المتفتتة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God restores each person's parts to their former arrangement and powers; the closing clause either confirms the argument or joins the relative clause.
rows.anchor: فيعيد كلا من ذلك على النمط السابق مع القوى التي كانت قبل والجملة إما اعتراض تذييلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominal sentence signals that God's knowledge is continuous, unlike His acts of creating particular things.
rows.anchor: والعدول إلى الإسمية للتنبيه على أن علمه تعالى بما ذكر أمر مستمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their astonishment is among the false claims that follow from arrogance and opposition.
rows.anchor: حكاية لأباطيلهم المتفرعة على ما حكاه من استكبارهم وشقاقهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They treat it as impossible that a messenger be their kind as a human or from their time and community, known for illiteracy; their wonder expresses emphatic denial.
rows.anchor: أي عجبوا من أن جاءهم رسول من جنسهم أي بشرا أو من عهدهم وهم معروفون بالأمية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explicit noun replaces a pronoun to condemn them, indicating only the deeply entrenched in unbelief and sin would dare say this.
rows.anchor: وضع فيه الظاهر موضع الضمير غضبا عليهم وذما لهم وإيذانا بأنه لا يتجاسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They call him a sorcerer because of signs he manifests that they cannot match.
rows.anchor: فيما يظهره مما لا نستطيع له مثلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They call him a liar for claiming that God sent and revealed to him.
rows.anchor: فيما يسنده إلى ألله عز وجل من الإرسال والإنزال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh leaders left Abu Talib's gathering after the Prophet rebuked them and they saw his firmness, having lost hope in his uncle's influence; they included Abu Jahl, al-As ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib ibn Abd Yaghuth, and Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt.
rows.anchor: الأشراف من قريش من مجلس أبي طالي

rows.speaker: أبو مجلز
rows.claim: Ibn Abi Hatim transmits from Abu Mijlaz that a man at Badr called them women; the Prophet replied they were the elite and recited this verse.
rows.anchor: عن أبي مجلز قال : قال رجل يوم بدر ما هم إلا النساء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent reading commands literal walking from the gathering, with explicative an introducing their words; one analysis supplies a suppressed state that the departing leaders were talking.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أنه أمر بالمشي بمعنى نقل الأقدام عن ذلك المجلس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another analysis needs no ellipsis: leaving a conversation naturally entails discussion among those departing, and context supplies the speech relation.
rows.anchor: وقيل لا حاجة إلى اعتبار الحذف فإن الإنطلاق عن مجلس التقاول يستلزم عادة تفاوض المنطلقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others take departure as a conventional metaphor for launching into speech, or as metaphorical attribution whose original sense is that their tongues set out.
rows.anchor: وقيل الإنطلاق هنا الإندفاع في القول فهو متضمن لمعنى القول بطريق الدلالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say walk means keep to your established way and persist in your practice.
rows.anchor: بعضهم : المراد بامشوا سيروا على طريقتكم وداوموا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another proposal connects imshu to prolific childbirth and abundant livestock, making the phrase an exhortation to multiply and gather.
rows.anchor: وقيل هو من مشت المرأة إذا كثرت ولادتها ومنه الماشية وسميت بذلك لأنها من شأنها كثرة الولادة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A proposal reads the phrase as a blessing for abundant cattle, an honorific opening; al-Alusi calls it erroneous because the verb needs a separating hamza and the sense is remote.
rows.anchor: افتتحوا به كلامهم للتعظيم كما يقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They urge one another to persist in worship of their gods and bear the criticism directed at them.
rows.anchor: أي اثبتوا على عبادتها متحملين لما تسمعونه في حقها من القدح

rows.speaker: عبدالله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud reads that they left walking, then said be steadfast; the walking clause is circumstantial or independent, and an is analyzed as in the standard reading.
rows.anchor: ابن مسعود ( وانطلق الملأ منهم
